attribution.note: Marcus's own bullet in his GPT-5 hot take post. He endorses it.

semantics.note: Faithful to the source. It keeps both the evaluative claim ('part of the pack, not a giant leap') and the ARC-AGI-2 example.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. It compares GPT-5 with frontier models available at launch, as the Grok 4 example implies. It allows GPT-5 to lead some evaluations and sets no invented threshold for 'giant'.

evidence.note: Launch-day post from the ARC Prize founder: Grok 4 at 15.9% vs GPT-5 at 9.9% on ARC-AGI-2. This confirms the example.

Independent launch evaluation. GPT-5 High sets a new index high (68), but the report calls the gain over o3 not comparable to earlier major jumps. That is a lead without clear separation from the frontier.
Later analysis (Aug 29, 2025) finding a large gain relative to GPT-4. That is a different baseline from the contract's contemporaneous one, so context only.

reviews.rationale: The ARC-AGI-2 ordering is confirmed by the benchmark operator. Independent launch measurement shows GPT-5 High narrowly leading an index, with a gain over o3 described as modest. That fits 'part of the pack, not a giant leap' under the contemporaneous baseline. Epoch's larger gain over GPT-4 uses a different baseline and does not meet the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own bullet in his GPT-5 hot take post. He endorses it.

semantics.note: The revision rightly removed 'to develop', which Marcus did not write. Duration, GPT-5 spending, and the fieldwide figure are all kept as he worded them.

contract.note: The contract chooses actual expenditure over funding or commitments and leaves the start date unspecified. Both are reasonable readings, and it openly flags them as interpretations Marcus did not supply.

evidence.note: GPT-4 release date (Mar 2023) from OpenAI. A possible starting point only; it does not show when GPT-5 development began.
GPT-5 launch announcement (Aug 7, 2025). Sets the endpoint, but gives no cost data.
Uncertain, projection-based estimates of OpenAI's company-wide R&D compute spending. These cannot establish GPT-5-specific or industry-wide spending.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only context items. Nothing establishes when GPT-5 development started, how much was spent on GPT-5, or a cumulative industry spending figure on a defined basis. Release dates alone cannot settle 'almost 3 years'. The evidence neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his GPT-5 hot take post. He endorses them.

semantics.note: Keeps 'appear', a provisional, evidence-based judgment rather than a probability hedge. 'I stand by' re-endorses his earlier predictions, some of which point to the future; the proposition rightly scores only the launch-state observation.

contract.note: Reading 'solved' as dependable resolution of each problem category, judged at launch, is fair. It properly sets aside parts of the earlier post that launch evidence cannot settle.

evidence.note: Marcus's July 27 post, which lists the problem categories. It is his own statement, so it cannot prove the outcome.
OpenAI's own disclosure, not an independent finding. It reports fewer hallucinations, not their elimination. That partly supports one category staying unsolved.
METR's launch evaluation finds genuine failures on autonomous tasks, which bears on reliability. It covers only some categories.

reviews.rationale: Support requires every applicable category to remain unsolved. The packet covers only hallucination and agentic reliability, and leaves out reasoning, guardrails, downstream integration, and the other categories. No evidence shows any category solved, so the claim is not contradicted. The packet does not settle the outcome.
